Regarding the practice of contemplating phenomena (*dharmānupaśyanā*):
although one has already known that unity and difference are empty, one has not yet spoken of how the objects of the emotions and the sensory dusts (*viṣaya*) are non-existent.

Now, wishing to traverse all phenomena to clarify emptiness so that the observing mind and the contacted objects may both be purified, the [text] next refutes the emotional objects and the sensory dusts.
Second, these arise from inverted and false conceptions that lack any fundamental basis;
they are produced through confusion.
When illness occurs, one should treat it immediately.
Each time it is rescued, it is immediately destroyed.
Therefore, while previously the fallacies of identity and difference were refuted, now the attachments of the sensory dust are cleansed.
Third, the Bodhisattva composed this treatise primarily to elucidate the sūtras.
Furthermore, the various Vaipulya sutras all clarify that the fundamental nature of the six sense-faculties is empty and quiescent;
however, these are explained diffusely throughout the scriptures.
Those of sharp faculties are able to realize this, while those of dull faculties have not yet understood it.
This chapter exists because we now provide a detailed explanation of this matter.
Fourth, because all sentient beings possess these mental states, they give rise to various afflictions (*kleśa*).
Those who live as householders give rise to craving (*tṛṣṇā*) due to their mental states and sensory objects (*viṣaya*).
The views of those non-Buddhist renunciants arise from the objects of the senses;
the same principle applies to the adherents of the Mahayana and Hinayana who hold to the notion of "attainment" within the Buddha-dharma.
Now, let us examine these objects of the senses.
Because there is ultimately nowhere from which they arise, the cravings and views of the large and small, the internal and external, come to rest;
therefore, this chapter exists.

Furthermore, all the Vaipulya sutras clarify that through the repentance of the six sense organs and the realization that the six are fundamentally empty, the offenses of the six sense organs are extinguished.
Fourth, because one performs repentance for the sake of those in the final age, one contemplates the emptiness of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*).
Furthermore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and other texts clarify the purity of the six sense faculties;
now, by awakening to the fundamental emptiness of the six [faculties], the six sense faculties become pure.
Now, in order to explain such sutras as these, I shall refute the six sense-faculties;
this is the general purpose [of my coming].
Next, as for the specific purpose:
Previously, by refuting both identity and difference, all phenomena were refuted in general;
for the meanings of both identity and difference between the myriad phenomena and the Great One (mahāsattva) are unestablished.
From this point onward, individual phenomena will be refuted specifically.
This refers to the causes and effects of sentient beings and their objects within the myriad phenomena;
the former is general while the latter is specific,
representing the sequential order of the gates of contemplation.
Furthermore, this chapter exists because it establishes the sequence of the thesis;
secondly, the preceding [section] refuted both identity and difference, thereby universally refuting both permanent and impermanent phenomena.
Now, the impermanent nature is specifically refuted;
this also follows the sequence of a general statement followed by a specific one.
Third, because the principle of identity and difference is obscured while the meaning of the sense objects (*viṣaya*) is manifest,
one abandons that [notion of] identity and difference and instead establishes the sense objects;
therefore, this chapter exists.
Fourth, the notions of identity and difference are exclusively the constructs of non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*).

Since both internal [mental] objects and external sensory spheres are clung to equally, these specific constructs cannot be established; therefore, he cites the general principle to provide a rebuttal.
Therefore, this chapter exists.

Fifth, at the end of the preceding "Refutation of the Heterogeneous" (Vaidharmya-dūṣaṇa), the author of the treatise rebuked the opponent, saying: "Those who see non-existence [as existence] and those who see existence [as non-existence].
Now, continuing from that point, he cites actual sentient beings and objects (*viṣaya*).
There is seeing existence,
yet it is not seeing non-existence as existence, nor is it seeing existence as non-existence.
If the Master were to refute the sensory objects (viṣaya), he would then see non-existence as existence and establish the Buddha-dharma separately.
This chapter exists because [people] see what does not exist. Previously,
the subjective mind was refuted, followed by the refutation of the objective realm.
The internal [subject] is the mind and the external [object] is the sense-field;
because their intimacy and distance differ, they are refuted as being either prior or posterior.
Question: Is the refutation of identity and difference now equivalent in meaning to the refutation of the mind and the sense-field?
Answer: From the perspective of the general principle, they are equal.
This is because non-Buddhists recklessly speculate on identity and difference, asserting that the Great Existence (mahāsattā) is either identical to or distinct from the myriad phenomena;
this too is a reckless speculation of the non-Buddhists.
The notions of partial creation and universal creation, as well as the perceptible objects such as jars, do not actually possess these properties.
Therefore, while the refutation of their meaning is essentially the same, there are slight differences:
the views of identity and difference are exclusively clung to by the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).
Therefore, it is said elsewhere:
"The *Mahābhūta-sūtra* of the non-Buddhists speaks of this [self], but we refute it and do not accept it.
If the objects of the senses were to penetrate both the internal and external," so it is stated.
Therefore, one both adopts and refutes.
If one were to arbitrarily claim that something exists,
then one would only refute it and not adopt it.
Because of causes and conditions, one grasps at provisional names and the objects of the senses without breaking them.
Question: What is the difference between the refutation of mental afflictions (*qing*) in this chapter and the refutation of mental afflictions in the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*?
Answer: The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* merely refutes the mental afflictions; it does not refute the meaning of the arising of cognition.
Now, [the meaning] is fully complete.

While the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* generally refutes the doctrine of views without separately distinguishing between "reaching" and "not reaching," this treatise specifically refutes the doctrine of reaching and not reaching. The reason for this is as follows:
The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* refutes the internal schools.
Since those of the internal schools— both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna— merely clarify that the non-attaining subject is able to see,
the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* directly refutes their view.
The externalists hold the views that [the self] either reaches [the object] or does not reach it when perceiving it;
therefore, this treatise fully refutes these two delusions.
As for what was said regarding "sentient beings":
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Among the ninety-six arts, consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is not mentioned;
because consciousness is difficult to understand, they explain only the five sense-faculties and the mind (*manas*)."
Because the deity dwells within the mental formations of the eye and other faculties, it is able to see forms.
Question: Since you state that non-Buddhists do not speak of the mental consciousness (manovijñāna), why do you say that the mental formations proceed through the gateway of the eye?
Answer: The non-Buddhists do not understand that mental consciousness arises from the mind-faculty (*manas*).
They merely claim that there is a "mind" which is the faculty of equanimity and name it the "mind.
They hold that the spirit (*ātman*) governs this mind as it proceeds through the gates of the eyes and other senses.
Now, regarding the statement "shattering emotional attachments," there are two meanings:
first, it directly shatters the six views of the non-Buddhists;
second, it indirectly shatters the internal adherents who recklessly claim there are six [views].
Second, whether internal or external, when these six sense organs (ṣaḍāyatana) exist, they are all said to give rise to the Buddha-dharma.
The *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* states:
"At the beginning of the kalpa, things had no names."
The Noble Ones provisionally establish names for the sake of conventional usage, such as "vase," "robe," and so forth.
Question: For what reason do the Noble Ones speak of six [bases]?
The answer is: The gates of the Dharma have never been six or not-six.
It is only because of inversion that one experiences these six sense organs.
The Sage desires to cause them to realize that these six do not exist.
Therefore, six are taught. As the Sūtra says:
"In order to bring about the realization of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) is taught.
For this reason, one is led to realize that the six [sense bases] are non-existent.
Sixth, the appearance in the world of all Buddhas of the three periods of time is solely for the sake of one great matter:
namely, to open, reveal, awaken, and lead others into the knowledge and vision of the Buddhas.
This knowledge and vision of the Buddhas is precisely the four wisdoms.
To contemplate that these six sense-faculties are fundamentally quiescent and extinguished is called the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
Although they are indeed quiescent, for sentient beings who are subject to delusion, these six faculties appear vividly as the very wisdom of the Buddha.
To realize that the six [objects] are not six is to understand that the non-existence of the six pairs manifests spontaneously; this is called "natural wisdom" (*svayambhū-jñāna*).
These three types of wisdom do not arise from a teacher and are thus termed "teacherless wisdom" (*aśaikṣa-jñāna*).
These four wisdoms constitute the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
It is because the Buddhas of the three periods of time wish to reveal, awaken to, and lead others into this wisdom and vision that they appear in the world.
These four wisdoms can be clearly understood wherever one encounters them.
However, taking the minds of sentient beings as the primary intent,
it is explained according to their emotional dispositions.
These dispositions are divided into two categories.
First, the refutation of the visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*); second, the application of this to the remaining five.
The first [section] further has two parts.
First, the refutation of the faculty so that cognition may arise.
Second is the correct refutation of conceptual clinging (*saṃjñā*).
The first part is the refutation of the effect, and the next is called the refutation of the cause.
Since both cause and effect have been refuted, all matters of conceptual clinging are exhausted.
The opponent says: "There must certainly be a self and phenomena belonging to a self, because they are presently manifest.
At the beginning of the previous chapter, the person was established by means of phenomena;
now, at the beginning of this chapter, phenomena are established by means of phenomena.
The phrase "there definitely exists that which belongs to a self" means that there is, for example, a single jar.

Regarding the phrase "because there is a phenomenon presently manifest," this cites the arising of cognition through the five sense faculties as proof for the existence of phenomena belonging to a self, such as a single jar.
"Manifest" refers to the five consciousnesses cognizing present phenomena.
Furthermore, manifest things are trustworthy;
who does not know blue and yellow?
Regarding what is called "knowing":
the six sense organs all involve a fourfold conjunction.
Within this fourfold conjunction, knowing arises; for example, when the eye conjoins with its object, one knows blue or yellow.
Up to the point where the mind (*manas*) and mental objects (*dharma*) come together, one is able to know those objects.
Now, the reason we take only the five types of cognition and do not discuss "mental cognition" (*mano-vijñāna*) is due to two reasons.
First, non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) do not speak of mental consciousness.
As explained above, secondly, the mental faculty (manas) perceives the three periods of time;

because it does not apprehend manifest phenomena, it is not mentioned [in the context of the sensory bases]. The five sense organs, in relation to the five objects, give rise to the five types of cognition.
This is mentioned specifically because it refers to the manifestation of phenomena (*dharmas*).
Question: Since this passage speaks of "knowledge arising," it appears to be a specific refutation of the Vaiśeṣika doctrine.
Answer: This correctly refutes the Vaiśeṣika by connecting with the preceding refutation of the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*).

Therefore, the objection raised by the World Teacher (the Vaiśeṣika)—that four [factors] arise together to produce cognition, and that while the former lacks vision it possesses existence, the latter possesses vision but lacks existence—is hereby refuted.
The Sāṃkhya school explains that because of the conjunction of conditions (*pratyaya-saṃyoga*), there is the function of cognition.
From the perspective of its functional utility (*artha-vṛtti*), one may indeed discuss its arising; however, its essence (*svabhāva*) does not arise.
Question: Why is it explained here that only these three must conjoin?
Answer: The opponent cites phenomena to prove phenomena and no longer applies further mental effort.
If one were to apply further mental effort, one would fall into defeat; therefore, he merely establishes the phenomenon (*dharma*).
If the meaning of the phenomenon is established, the meaning of the person (*pudgala*) is established of its own accord.
Therefore, the text states: "It is certain that there is what belongs to a self.
The internal [opponent] says: "Since one has already known the arising of form through vision, what further use is there?
The internal refutation of the arising of knowledge has three gates.
This refers to the simultaneity of the preceding and the succeeding.
Here, the view that the preceding [perception] is followed by a subsequent cognition is refuted.
Originally, for one who has not yet seen colors such as blue or yellow, there must be a cognition of blue or yellow.
Now, since one clearly perceives blue and yellow with the eye, one knows that [the existence of] a "birth" (jāti) is useless;
this directly refutes the doctrine of the Sāṃkhyas.
Since the visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) is already capable of seeing form, [what further need is there for a separate "birth"?]
What is the use of consciousness?
If it must rely on consciousness to discern blue or yellow,
how can it be called "seeing with the eye"?
If it were the case that seeing occurs only when visual consciousness is in conjunction [with the eye],
this would contradict the established tenet that the eye itself is capable of seeing.
Furthermore, if prior cognition arises first and subsequent seeing follows, this constitutes the second refutation of the claim that prior cognition precedes seeing.
However, one knows first and sees later;
thus, knowing has utility.
But because seeing is absent, knowing cannot arise.
Secondly, there is further the fault of contradicting your own tenet.
You claim that cognition arises from the conjunction of the four;
yet now, cognition arises even though the four have not yet conjoined.
Therefore, it contradicts the previous thesis.
Previously, one understood that the thesis fell into futility;
now, one understands that while it possesses utility, it falls into contradicting the thesis.
The opponent says: "If they arise simultaneously,
[we] defend this by saying that one knows their arising at the very moment one sees the form."
Since one perceives form at the very moment of its arising, the two aforementioned faults do not apply.
Question: Why is there no *sūtra* [to explain this]?
The answer has two meanings.
First, the opponent previously established a single present cognition,
to which Deva formulated three successive difficulties.
This refers to [the fault of] simultaneity between the preceding and the succeeding.
However, because Vasubandhu intended to formulate a refutation of simultaneity, this point arose as an external objection;
therefore, it does not appear in the sūtra.
Furthermore, because it is easily understood, it is not explained;
this is why it is absent.
The internal [commentary] states that the following verse originally consisted of four [lines].
First, the citation; second, the refutation; third, the objection; fourth, the explanation.
"If they were produced simultaneously" is the citation.
"This matter is not so" is the refutation.
The third difficulty concerns the impossibility of arising and non-arising occurring simultaneously.
Question: On what basis is this difficulty raised?
Answer: It is raised specifically from the perspective of the gate of non-arising, because the opponent asserts that they arise simultaneously.
Now, if one merely negates its arising, it collapses simultaneously of its own accord.
Furthermore, since arising extends across both the prior and subsequent moments,
negating arising at this present moment effectively negates all three meanings [of time] together.
Furthermore, if one were merely to refute the perception of simultaneity, one would not be able to simultaneously refute other phenomena.
Now, by refuting arising, one simultaneously reveals that all phenomena are non-arising.
Because [phenomena] exist, because they do not exist, and because they have been previously refuted, this constitutes the fourth explanation of the refutation.
Because of existence, the "arising from above" is explained;
because of non-existence, the "non-arising" is explained;
because the former was refuted, the "common [arising]" is explained.
However, there are two ways in which the prior [position] is refuted.
First, because existence and non-existence are considered "prior" in relation to their conjunction,
the refutation of existence and non-existence is called the refutation of conjunction.
Second, according to Vasubandhu, the first two verses are designated as "common.
The first verse refutes the view that there is prior perception followed by subsequent cognition;
this [position] maintains that there is perception but no cognition.
The next verse refutes the [position] that there is prior cognition and subsequent seeing,
which implies there is cognition but no seeing.
Since the previous two [positions] have already been refuted, the negation of both existence and non-existence is termed the "refutation of the conjunction" (*sādhāraṇa*).
Therefore, it is said that the former has been refuted.
Furthermore, the root verse clearly states "because of existence" and "because of non-existence";
these two are precisely two sūtras.
It refers back to these two, hence it is called "the two sūtras.
In the commentary, they are divided into two parts:
the first explains the verses and their primary meaning, while the second refutes the [notion of] simultaneity.
The reason for clarifying these two points is that [the opponent] externally posits arising at a single time,
while the root verse refutes that arising.
If the meaning of Vasubandhu refutes [the position that] things exist simultaneously,
then these two meanings are exhausted.
The first [section] further has three [parts].
First, the restatement.
Following this, the next section provides a general negation of the three [positions].
As for the subsequent section, it constitutes the formal refutation of the latter three.
Furthermore, if they were simultaneous, the second meaning would refute simultaneity:
seeing is the cause,
and knowing is called the fruit.
If one knows and sees at the same time, then the principle of mutual dependence is simultaneously lost.
Furthermore, does the eye see by reaching the object?
From the preceding discussion upward, the doctrine that cognition arises [from contact] has been refuted.
Now, for the second time, his views are refuted through three gates:
first, the gate of reaching and not reaching;
second, the refutation that the nature of the eye sees itself.
The threefold refutation concerning whether [the eye] reaches or does not reach its object reveals that the doctrines of the internal schools regarding the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna differ; all, however,
maintain that the eye perceives by gazing from afar without reaching the object.
The Sāṃkhya school also says that the eye can gaze out freely.
Therefore, when the eye encounters an evil matter, one must avoid it;
when encountering a good matter, one must approach it.
The same applies to the ear hearing sounds;
this is entirely identical to the Buddha’s teaching.
As for the three faculties of nose, tongue, and body, because they constitute the physical body, they must reach the object before cognition occurs.
The same applies to the internal meaning.
Now, Deva, in order to comprehensively refute the various schools, opens two avenues of inquiry to censure them.
First, the refutation of the view that [the self] reaches form is easy to understand.
Furthermore, when the lower heaven seeks to refute the higher heaven’s view that [the object] reaches [the eye], and [the proponent] establishes the view that it does not reach [the eye],
there should be four objections: first,
since both [the near and the far] would equally not reach [the eye], they should both be invisible.
2. If both the near and the distant are equally unattainable, then one should see both.
3. If one sees the near but does not see the distant, then one should reach the near but not reach the distant.
4. If one sees the near but does not see the distant, then one should see the distant but not see the near.
Furthermore, the subsequent section opens two gates to re-examine the meaning of reaching the object of visual perception.
It first states:
"If one perceives the form and only then departs, one falls into the error of futility."
If one departs without seeing, one would possess the function of seeing while contradicting what is intended by the object of apprehension.

Furthermore, even in the absence of the locus of the eye, one does not apprehend [the object]; thus, two further gates are opened to refute both the reaching and the non-reaching [of the sense organ].
The first [section] clarifies that if the eye were to go to the object in order to apprehend it, the face would lose its possession of the eye;
the latter [section] clarifies that while the face does not lose its possession of the eye, it loses the capacity for apprehension.
Furthermore, there are four further refutations against the position that the eye does not reach the object:

first, if it were equally unable to reach [the object], then there would be no distinction between seeing what is obstructed and what is not; second, one would see both the internal and the external simultaneously; third, one would see nothing at all; fourth, [the eye] would see everything.
Third, regarding the obstruction of vision: if one does not see the external while looking internally, one should likewise see the internal while looking externally.
Fourth, there is the case of seeing versus not seeing, and reaching versus not reaching;
for both the internal and external schools maintain that [the eye] does not reach its object.
One should refute this through detailed analysis.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"If one were to go and see it, the eye seeing the fire now would be burned by that fire."
If the eye were to see water, the water should moisten the eye.
This is explained in the twenty-eighth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*,
which states that one knows the mental inclinations of sentient beings.
The opponent asks:

Second, the preceding refutation of the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) refutes the doctrines of the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* and other schools.

As for your sutra's statement that "form" refers to the four great elements and that which is derived from the four great elements, I shall now briefly present four schools of tenets.

There are cases where the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), which possess identical characteristics, produce derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) that possesses different characteristics.
That is to say, the four great elements are all "tangible objects" (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*) and are thus termed "identical characteristics";
however, the derived matter they produce—such as color, fragrance, and so forth—is termed "different characteristics."
There are cases where the four great elements of a similar nature produce matter of a similar nature;
the four great elements, being of the nature of tangibility, in turn produce tangibility.
There are also cases where the four great elements of a dissimilar nature produce matter of a dissimilar nature.
The four great elements each produce derived matter (upādāya-rūpa) such as color and fragrance, as fully explained in the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya*.
Question: Among the six causes, which cause is it that produces derived matter from the four great elements?
Answer: It is merely the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
Question: Among the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*), which creates the four great elements?
Answer: Formerly, some people said: [text continues]
The three great elements create one great element.
The master of mirrors said:

The *Abhidharmavibhāṣā-śāstra* provides one explanation, stating:

Among the divisions of derived matter, that which is subsumed under the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*) is what is directly perceived.
The primary elements that constitute [matter] are themselves invisible;
among the derived forms, there are two types.
If it belongs to the sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*), then it is visible.

The opponent says: Because there is the experiencing of the new and the old, the present time exists.
Having previously used the concepts of the new and the old to refute the present, the opponent then asserts:
The Master of the Treatise accepts their [distinction between] the new and the old.
If there is the new and the old, then there are two implications:
first, since there is the new and the old, there must be a beginning and an end, and consequently, there must be an intermediate present.
Second, since one grasps the new and the old, it must necessarily occur at a present time;
and since there is that which is grasped as new and old, there must necessarily be a time for grasping the new and the old.
The internal [objection] says: "The arising of the old is different from the new, and thus it is old."
Previously, the new was refuted by means of the old and the present;
now, the new and the old are refuted.
That which is produced as "old" refutes the "new."
Regarding your statement that what has just arisen is "new":
it follows that a phenomenon (dharma) at the very moment of its initial arising must be new.
Since your "new" phenomenon emerges from emptiness and enters into existence, it is designated as "new."
Therefore, dharmas likewise initially emerge from emptiness and enter into existence;
how could this not be "new"?
Herein lie four difficulties.
First, if both emerge together from emptiness and enter into existence, they should be equally new.
Second, they should be equally old.
Third, if one considers the former to be new and the latter to be old, [this would be inconsistent].
Furthermore, that which comes later should be the new and that which comes first should be the old.
Fourth, since you maintain that there is both the new and the old, there must be both that which is born at the beginning and that which is not born at the beginning;
because they are distinct, the "old" is thereby refuted.
The new and the contrary are different; this is why they are so.
What fixed principle is there?
The commentary is divided into two parts:
first, the formal refutation of the new and the old;
second, the conclusion that returns to the ultimate and the conventional.
The first section also has two parts.
The former pursues the explanation of the distinction between the old and the new;
the latter explains how the new arises from the old through the sequence of their mutual production.
This concludes by returning to the two truths, as the text states.
An opponent asks: "If that is so, what benefit is gained?"
From the beginning up to this point, two chapters have refuted the doctrine of non-temporal dharmas.
Now, for the third time, the benefits derived [from the teaching] are clarified.
As for the origin of this passage, there are both distant and proximate antecedents.
As for the distant [objections], everything from the first chapter up to this chapter has been refuted;
what benefit is there [in further discussion]?
As for the proximate [objection], the outsider claims that dharmas possess four temporal stages through which they may benefit sentient beings.
Now that this no longer exists, what benefit is obtained?
The internal [response] says: "One obtains permanent liberation."
The non-Buddhists have a deep-seated attachment to phenomena;
therefore, it is now clarified that attachment itself is bondage, while detachment results in liberation.
As for the expression "permanently detached":
The non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) sever their fetters with the sense of a temporary liberation, yet they ultimately regress.
By turning away from the heterodox and entering the correct path, one attains permanent liberation.

Furthermore, from the first stage through this chapter, it is clarified that there is no longer any bondage of attainment for ordinary beings or those of the two vehicles; this constitutes ultimate and permanent liberation.
When one is detached from attachments, all burdens are stilled;
thus, virtue becomes perfectly complete, and one realizes the Dharma-body of the Middle Way.
Furthermore, because one does not perceive new things, one knows that things are empty.
When one does not perceive the new person nor the old person, one knows that persons are empty.
Because awakening to these two emptinesses destroys all afflictions, it is called "eternal liberation.
Furthermore, because [these two] are the causes of the two types of birth and death.
The second death-result is new;
apart from this cause and effect, everything is detached.

Regarding the long passage which says, "the new does not produce the middle, nor does the middle produce the middle": [this means that the new result does not arise from the middle state, nor does the middle state arise from the middle state].
From ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*), one newly experiences five fruits; this is called "newly produced in the middle.
Because the three causes of the present produce two fruits in the future, it is called "produced in the middle.
Therefore, the twelve links of dependent origination consist of only two divisions.
The seven [links] constitute the prior portion and the five constitute the posterior portion;
just as there are seeds, sprouts, stalks, and nodes,
the twelve links of dependent origination are like a great tree.
The two causes are the roots and the five fruits are the essence; the three causes are the flowers and the two fruits are the fruit.
Once the essence of the roots has perished, the flower and the fruit cannot coincide.
Therefore, the simile of the grain seed is employed here.
